1: # Tic-Tac-Toe, No Draws — playable game
2: 
3: Status: ready-for-agent
4: 
5: ## Problem Statement
6: 
7: A candidate exercise asks for a two-player 3×3 tic-tac-toe variant in which a game can never
8: end in a draw and every line of play terminates. The rule has been chosen and stated
9: (`docs/RULES.md`), and the exhaustive evidence that it works has been recorded
10: (`docs/research/no-draw-variants.md`), but there is no game to play and no design document
11: arguing that the implementation matches the rule. A reviewer opening the repo can read a rule
12: but cannot play it, and cannot see why it is correct.
13: 
14: ## Solution
15: 
16: A static, dependency-free browser game that implements the stated variant exactly: X moves
17: first, three of a player's own marks in a line is a line win, and a **fill win** goes to O when
18: the board fills with no line. A line completed on the ninth move still wins outright. A draw is
19: not a reachable outcome, and the interface cannot present one.
20: 
21: All rule logic lives in a single pure, DOM-free engine module; the interface layer only renders
22: the board and the engine's status and forwards clicks. A winning line is highlighted, and a fill
23: win is presented distinctly from a line win so the variant is visible in play. `docs/DESIGN.md`
24: records the reading of the brief, the rejected rule sets, and the argument that draws are
25: impossible and play always terminates.
26: 
27: ## User Stories
28: 
29: 1. As a player, I want to take turns placing marks on a 3×3 board, so that I can play a game of
30:    tic-tac-toe.
31: 2. As X, I want to move first, so that the game follows tic-tac-toe convention.
32: 3. As a player, I want to place my mark in any empty cell, so that I can pursue a line.
33: 4. As a player, I want the game to refuse a mark on an occupied cell, so that I cannot overwrite
34:    an existing mark.
35: 5. As a player, I want to see whose turn it is, so that I know when to move.
36: 6. As a player, I want to win by completing a line of three of my own marks, so that I get the
37:    standard tic-tac-toe win.
38: 7. As X, I want a line I complete on the ninth move to win outright, so that the fill rule never
39:    steals a win I have earned.
40: 8. As O, I want to win when the board fills with no line, so that a lineless full board still
41:    produces a winner.
42: 9. As a player, I want the game to announce the winner, so that I know the game has ended.
43: 10. As a player, I want the announcement to say whether the game ended in a line win or a fill
44:     win, so that I can see the variant working rather than taking it on faith.
45: 11. As a player, I want the winning line highlighted when a line win occurs, so that I can see
46:     why the game ended.
47: 12. As a player, I want a fill win to look different from a line win, so that I can tell there
48:     was no line at all.
49: 13. As a player, I want to start a new game, so that I can play again after a game ends.
50: 14. As a player, I want a new game to reset the board completely, so that no marks carry over.
51: 15. As a player, I want to be unable to place a mark after the game has ended, so that a
52:     terminal position cannot change.
53: 16. As a player, I want never to see a draw, because the variant guarantees every game has a
54:     winner.
55: 17. As a player, I want every game to end within nine moves, so that play always terminates.
56: 18. As the candidate, I want the rules stated plainly enough for a stranger to play from a
57:     printed copy, so that the variant needs no reference to the code.
58: 19. As the candidate, I want the engine to be the only place rules live, so that the interface
59:     layer cannot contradict the rule or drift from it.
60: 20. As the candidate, I want the engine to be pure and DOM-free, so that its behaviour can be
61:     reasoned about in isolation from rendering.
62: 21. As the candidate, I want the engine's state to be immutable, so that a move produces a new
63:     position and earlier positions cannot be corrupted.
64: 22. As the candidate, I want an illegal move to throw rather than be silently ignored, so that
65:     mistakes surface instead of hiding.
66: 23. As the candidate, I want terminal states to have no legal moves, so that the engine itself
67:     makes continuing a finished game impossible.
68: 24. As the reviewer, I want `docs/DESIGN.md` to record my reading of the brief and the
69:     ambiguities I resolved, so that my decisions are defensible without me in the room.
70: 25. As the reviewer, I want `docs/DESIGN.md` to list the rule sets I considered and rejected,
71:     with reasons and measured numbers, so that the chosen rule is visibly a considered choice.
72: 26. As the reviewer, I want `docs/DESIGN.md` to argue that draws are impossible and that play
73:     always terminates, backed by the exhaustive enumeration already in the repo, so that the
74:     correctness claim is supported rather than asserted.
75: 27. As the reviewer, I want `docs/DESIGN.md` to state anything that is broken or unfinished, so
76:     that I am not misled about the state of the work.
77: 28. As the candidate, I want the ADR to record why a lineless full board is awarded to O, so
78:     that the most surprising part of the rule is explained to future readers.
79: 29. As an agent working on this repo, I want `AGENTS.md` to state how to run the game and the
80:     conventions to follow, so that future sessions respect the engine/interface seam.
81: 30. As an agent working on this repo, I want the glossary in `CONTEXT.md`, so that I name domain
82:     concepts consistently with the rest of the project.
83: 31. As a reviewer, I want to run the game with a static server and no build step, so that
84:     trying it out takes one command.
85: 32. As a reviewer, I want the game to work in current Chrome with no dependencies or network
86:     calls, so that nothing needs installing.
87: 
88: ## Implementation Decisions
89: 
90: - **Rule authority.** `docs/RULES.md` remains the single source of truth. The engine encodes
91:   that rule and nothing else; if the rule changes, `docs/RULES.md` changes first.
92: - **One engine module, pure and DOM-free.** It owns every rule decision: legal moves, turn
93:   order, line wins, the fill win, and the precedence of a ninth-move line over the fill rule.
94:   It is an ESM module, browser-only, with immutable state transitions.
95: - **Engine interface contract** (from the design session; the exact shape encodes decisions that
96:   prose would blur):
97: 
98:   ```
99:   createGame()                      -> State
100:   board(state)                      -> ReadonlyArray<'X' | 'O' | null>
101:   currentPlayer(state)              -> 'X' | 'O'
102:   legalMoves(state)                 -> number[]            // empty iff terminal
103:   applyMove(state, cell)            -> State               // immutable; throws on illegal
104:   status(state)                     -> {
105:                                          over: boolean,
106:                                          winner: 'X' | 'O' | null,
107:                                          reason: 'line' | 'fill' | null,
108:                                          line: [number, number, number] | null,
109:                                          moveCount: number
110:                                        }
111:   ```
112: 
113:   `State` is opaque to the interface layer, which must not read it directly. `reason: 'fill'`
114:   can only ever accompany a win by O. `line` holds the three cells of a line win and drives the
115:   highlight; it is `null` for a fill win.
116: - **One interface module, no logic.** It renders the board from `board(state)`, renders whose
117:   turn it is from `currentPlayer(state)`, forwards clicks to `applyMove`, and renders the
118:   result from `status(state)`. It performs no rule check of any kind — in particular it does not
119:   decide whether a move is legal or who has won.
120: - **Winning-line highlight** is driven entirely by `status.line`. A fill win gets a distinct
121:   treatment (the whole board is indicated as full with no line) so the two endings are visually
122:   different.
123: - **New Game** calls `createGame()` for a fresh State; there is no separate reset path.
124: - **Illegal clicks** (occupied or terminal cells) must not mutate state; the interface ignores
125:   them and the engine's `applyMove` throws if one is ever attempted.
126: - **No build step, no dependencies, no network, no backend.** Browser-only ESM served by
127:   `python3 -m http.server`. No transpiling or polyfills; current Chrome only.
128: - **Documentation deliverables.** `docs/DESIGN.md` is written to cover the brief's four required
129:   areas: reading of the brief and ambiguities resolved; rejected rule sets and why; the
130:   no-draw and termination argument; and known unfinished work. The argument is informal prose
131:   that cites the exhaustive enumeration already committed under `docs/research/`.
132: - **Already produced by the design phase, not part of this spec's tickets:** `docs/RULES.md`,
133:   `docs/research/no-draw-variants.md`, `CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/0001-lineless-full-board-awarded-to-o.md`,
134:   `AGENTS.md`, and the issue-tracker configuration under `docs/agents/`.
135: 
136: ## Testing Decisions
137: 
138: - **What makes a good test here:** one that asserts externally observable engine behaviour over
139:   the real reachable game tree, never internal representation. A test that inspects a State's
140:   internals, or that re-derives a rule, is testing implementation detail and is wrong.
141: - **No automated test runner is introduced.** By decision, the correctness argument is informal
142:   prose in `docs/DESIGN.md`, backed by the exhaustive enumeration of the *rule* already recorded
143:   in `docs/research/no-draw-variants.md` (all 255,168 lines of play, zero draws, maximum length
144:   9). The brief does not score test coverage beyond what supports this argument.
145: - **The one seam** is the engine's public interface above. It is the highest seam available —
146:   the interface module is deliberately logic-free, so there is nothing meaningful to assert
147:   there. If automated verification is ever added, it targets this seam and nothing else,
148:   exhaustively: walk every legal line of play from `createGame()` via `legalMoves`/`applyMove`
149:   and assert that every terminal state has a non-null `winner`, that `legalMoves` is empty at
150:   terminal states, and that no line of play exceeds nine moves.
151: - **Prior art:** the Python exhaustive solver embedded in `docs/research/no-draw-variants.md`
152:   is the model for such a check, and the numbers `docs/DESIGN.md` cites.
153: 
154: ## Out of Scope
155: 
156: - A computer opponent. Explicitly optional and not scored by the brief.
157: - Undo, move history, running score, and any multi-game tracking.
158: - Visual polish: animation, sound, responsive layout, and accessibility work are not scored.
159: - Automated tests and any test runner or Node tooling.
160: - Transcript export, `transcript/README.md`, and commit boundaries — handled by the candidate
161:   outside this spec; commits are made per ticket.
162: - Changes to the rule itself. The rule is frozen in `docs/RULES.md`; this spec implements it.
163: 
164: ## Further Notes
165: 
166: - **Why the fill win goes to O** is recorded in ADR-0001. In short: keeping the standard line
167:   win forces a decision on the lineless full board, and awarding it to O is the smallest change
168:   with the best casual balance. Because X moves first and nine is odd, the ninth move is always
169:   X's, so "the board fills with no line, O wins" is equivalently "the ninth move loses".
170: - **Perfect-play balance is impossible** in any no-draw variant: Zermelo determinacy means
171:   exactly one player has a forced win. Under this rule that player is O. "Balance" is therefore
172:   claimed only empirically — X 58.5% / O 41.5% under uniform random play — and `docs/DESIGN.md`
173:   must not overclaim it.
174: - **Termination is structural, not probabilistic:** every move occupies one previously empty
175:   cell, with no passing, capture, or removal, so the game is a DAG graded by mark count and
176:   cannot exceed nine moves.
177: - The 16 historically drawn full boards are reclassified as fill wins for O; all 16 are
178:   reachable in normal play.
179: - The engine must be able to represent only terminal positions that have a winner; a draw is not
180:   a runtime concept in this project (see `CONTEXT.md`).

(End of file - total 180 lines)
</content>

  that rule and nothing else; if the rule changes, `docs/RULES.md` changes first.
- **One engine module, pure and DOM-free.** It owns every rule decision: legal moves, turn
  order, line wins, the fill win, and the precedence of a ninth-move line over the fill rule.
  It is an ESM module, browser-only, with immutable state transitions.
- **Engine interface contract** (from the design session; the exact shape encodes decisions that
  prose would blur):

  ```
  createGame()                      -> State
  board(state)                      -> ReadonlyArray<'X' | 'O' | null>
  currentPlayer(state)              -> 'X' | 'O'
  legalMoves(state)                 -> number[]            // empty iff terminal
  applyMove(state, cell)            -> State               // immutable; throws on illegal
  status(state)                     -> {
                                         over: boolean,
                                         winner: 'X' | 'O' | null,
                                         reason: 'line' | 'fill' | null,
                                         line: [number, number, number] | null,
                                         moveCount: number
                                       }
  ```

  `State` is opaque to the interface layer, which must not read it directly. `reason: 'fill'`
  can only ever accompany a win by O. `line` holds the three cells of a line win and drives the
  highlight; it is `null` for a fill win.
- **One interface module, no logic.** It renders the board from `board(state)`, renders whose
  turn it is from `currentPlayer(state)`, forwards clicks to `applyMove`, and renders the
  result from `status(state)`. It performs no rule check of any kind — in particular it does not
  decide whether a move is legal or who has won.
- **Winning-line highlight** is driven entirely by `status.line`. A fill win gets a distinct
  treatment (the whole board is indicated as full with no line) so the two endings are visually
  different.
- **New Game** calls `createGame()` for a fresh State; there is no separate reset path.
- **Illegal clicks** (occupied or terminal cells) must not mutate state; the interface ignores
  them and the engine's `applyMove` throws if one is ever attempted.
- **No build step, no dependencies, no network, no backend.** Browser-only ESM served by
  `python3 -m http.server`. No transpiling or polyfills; current Chrome only.
- **Documentation deliverables.** `docs/DESIGN.md` is written to cover the brief's four required
  areas: reading of the brief and ambiguities resolved; rejected rule sets and why; the
  no-draw and termination argument; and known unfinished work. The argument is informal prose
  that cites the exhaustive enumeration already committed under `docs/research/`.
- **Already produced by the design phase, not part of this spec's tickets:** `docs/RULES.md`,
  `docs/research/no-draw-variants.md`, `CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/0001-lineless-full-board-awarded-to-o.md`,
  `AGENTS.md`, and the issue-tracker configuration under `docs/agents/`.

## Testing Decisions

- **What makes a good test here:** one that asserts externally observable engine behaviour over
  the real reachable game tree, never internal representation. A test that inspects a State's
  internals, or that re-derives a rule, is testing implementation detail and is wrong.
- **No automated test runner is introduced.** By decision, the correctness argument is informal
  prose in `docs/DESIGN.md`, backed by the exhaustive enumeration of the *rule* already recorded
  in `docs/research/no-draw-variants.md` (all 255,168 lines of play, zero draws, maximum length
  9). The brief does not score test coverage beyond what supports this argument.
- **The one seam** is the engine's public interface above. It is the highest seam available —
  the interface module is deliberately logic-free, so there is nothing meaningful to assert
  there. If automated verification is ever added, it targets this seam and nothing else,
  exhaustively: walk every legal line of play from `createGame()` via `legalMoves`/`applyMove`
  and assert that every terminal state has a non-null `winner`, that `legalMoves` is empty at
  terminal states, and that no line of play exceeds nine moves.
- **Prior art:** the Python exhaustive solver embedded in `docs/research/no-draw-variants.md`
  is the model for such a check, and the numbers `docs/DESIGN.md` cites.

## Out of Scope

- A computer opponent. Explicitly optional and not scored by the brief.
- Undo, move history, running score, and any multi-game tracking.
- Visual polish: animation, sound, responsive layout, and accessibility work are not scored.
- Automated tests and any test runner or Node tooling.
- Transcript export, `transcript/README.md`, and commit boundaries — handled by the candidate
  outside this spec; commits are made per ticket.
- Changes to the rule itself. The rule is frozen in `docs/RULES.md`; this spec implements it.

## Further Notes

- **Why the fill win goes to O** is recorded in ADR-0001. In short: keeping the standard line
  win forces a decision on the lineless full board, and awarding it to O is the smallest change
  with the best casual balance. Because X moves first and nine is odd, the ninth move is always
  X's, so "the board fills with no line, O wins" is equivalently "the ninth move loses".
- **Perfect-play balance is impossible** in any no-draw variant: Zermelo determinacy means
  exactly one player has a forced win. Under this rule that player is O. "Balance" is therefore
  claimed only empirically — X 58.5% / O 41.5% under uniform random play — and `docs/DESIGN.md`
  must not overclaim it.
- **Termination is structural, not probabilistic:** every move occupies one previously empty
  cell, with no passing, capture, or removal, so the game is a DAG graded by mark count and
  cannot exceed nine moves.
- The 16 historically drawn full boards are reclassified as fill wins for O; all 16 are
  reachable in normal play.
- The engine must be able to represent only terminal positions that have a winner; a draw is not
  a runtime concept in this project (see `CONTEXT.md`).

A two-player tic-tac-toe variant whose entire reason to exist is that every game ends with a
winner: X moves first and must complete a line, and a board that fills with no line is awarded
to O.

## Language

**Board**:
The 3×3 grid of nine cells; together with whose turn it is, the whole state of a game.

**Mark**:
An X or an O occupying a cell. X always moves first, so X places on moves 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, and

_Avoid_: Piece, token, stone

win can be completed. Use "row", "column" and "diagonal" only when the orientation matters.
_Avoid_: Three-in-a-row (as a name for the cells themselves)

A player wins by placing a mark that completes a line of three of their own marks.
_Avoid_: Normal win, standard win

O wins because the board reaches nine marks with no line. At most one fill win can occur in a
game, and it is always X that has just moved, so a fill win is equivalently "the ninth move
loses".

A position in which the game has ended — by either a line win or a fill win.

Closeness of the two players' win rates. Two senses must not be conflated: *perfect-play

moves) and is the sense in which this variant is defended.
